newsitem.title: CHINA: Amnesty tells China to reconsider 1989 crackdown.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty tells China to reconsider 1989 crackdown.

text.p: Human rights group Amnesty International called on China on Tuesday to take the chance afforded by the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping to reconsider its 1989 crackdown on pro-democracy protests.

In a statement released before the eighth anniversary of the crushing of the student-led demonstrations on June 4, Amnesty said China continued to harass both relatives bereaved by the bloody crackdown and dissidents who commemorated the date.

"Eight years after the brutal suppression of the 1989 pro-democracy movement, the time has come for the Chinese government to re-evaluate the events, account for the hundreds who died and free the many who remain in jail for their part in the protests," Amnesty said.

This year's anniversary is the first since the death in February of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, who put the final seal of approval on the use of soldiers and tanks to crush pro-democracy protests centred on Beijing's Tiananmen Square.
Analysts say Deng's death at 92 could give his political heirs more freedom of action on how to deal with the thorny legacy of the Tiananmen pro-democracy movement.
Beijing has stuck to its line that tough action was needed to end a counter-revolutionary rebellion sparked by student protests against corruption, inflation and state censorship.

Dissidents, relatives of those killed and many ordinary Beijing residents have long yearned for a reversal of the official judgement on the crackdown that would recognise the dead as patriots rather than criminals.

"Following the death of Deng Xiaoping, the new leadership should take the opportunity to re-evaluate the events of 1989 and end the distorted and inaccurate propaganda of the last eight years," Amnesty said.
"The victims and their families deserve the truth at long last, rather than the harassment, surveillance and attempts to silence their brave struggle for truth and justice," it said.
The international rights watchdog welcomed reports that four dissidents jailed in northeastern Jilin after protesting the June 4 crackdown had had their convictions overturned.
"We hope this is a sign that the government may be prepared to review the hundreds of other cases of people who were jailed during the 1989 crackdown," it said.

Amnesty's call for a re-appraisal of the use of force, which left hundreds of students, workers and residents dead, came after bereaved relatives sent a petition appealing to China's parliament for an official enquiry into the action.

The petition sent by 42 relatives to the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress also called for a direct and sincere dialogue with the parliament, which has ignored similar requests in the last two years.
By sending tanks against unarmed students, the Chinese government had committed a crime against its own people, said one of the signatories, retired associate professor of philosophy Ding Zilin.

Remaining anger at the June 4 crackdown has cast a shadow over the July 1 return to Chinese sovereignty of the British colony of Hong Kong, where protests against Beijing have been an annual fixture since 1989.
More than 3,500 Hong Kong protesters defied their future ruler on Sunday by marching along the territory's main street to mourn the dead and demand the official verdict be reconsidered.
Protestors waved banners calling for the release of jailed dissidents and some bore a coffin on which was painted "the butcher government will remain notorious for a million years".
